title: Oxidation states and half-equations; Oxidation states and naming

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Metal hydride
items.clue: Compound such as NaH or CaH₂ in which H is −1.

items.label: Peroxide
items.clue: Compound such as H₂O₂ or Na₂O₂ in which O is −1.

items.label: Oxidation number
items.clue: The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic.

items.label: Redox
items.clue: A reaction in which loss and gain of electrons happen together.

questions.stem: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻(aq) oxidizes Fe²⁺(aq) to Fe³⁺(aq) and is itself reduced to Mn²⁺(aq). Which equation is the balanced net ionic equation for the reaction? (States are omitted; all ions are aqueous and H₂O is liquid.)

options.text: MnO₄⁻ + 8 H⁺ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H₂O + Fe³⁺
MnO₄⁻ + 8 H⁺ + 5 Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H₂O + 5 Fe³⁺
MnO₄⁻ + 8 H⁺ + Fe²⁺ + 4 e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H₂O + Fe³⁺

questions.explanation: MnO₄⁻ + 8 H⁺ + 5 e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4 H₂O, and each Fe²⁺ loses one electron, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed. The total charge is +17 on each side.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of carbon in the oxalate ion, C₂O₄²⁻?
questions.explanation: Each O is −2 and the oxidation numbers add up to the ion's charge: 2x + 4(−2) = −2, so the two C atoms total +6 and each is +3.

questions.stem: In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). What happens to the iron?

options.text: It loses electrons: iron is always oxidised when it reacts, as it does in rusting.
It gains electrons: its oxidation number falls from +3 to 0, and aluminium supplies them.
It loses electrons to aluminium, since aluminium gains the oxygen during the reaction.
It gains electrons: its oxidation number falls from +6 to 0, as Fe₂O₃ has two Fe atoms.

questions.stem: Chlorine is −1 in the chloride ion, Cl⁻, but +1 in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻ (in bleach). Which explains the +1?

options.text: The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ has lost a proton to the oxygen atom, leaving chlorine with a +1 charge.
Oxygen always has the oxidation number −1 in an ion with one negative charge.
Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so it is assigned the shared electrons in the Cl–O bond.
The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ carries a real charge of +1, as in a Cl⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: O takes both shared electrons and is −2; the total must be −1, so x + (−2) = −1 and Cl is +1. In Cl⁻, chlorine holds an extra electron: −1.
